result: The manuscript provides background on opsin classification and properties. Opsins are universal photoreceptive G-protein-coupled receptors found in animals, classified into three types based on photoreaction properties: monostable (vertebrate rhodopsin), bistable (mollusk/arthropod rhodopsins), and photocyclic (Opn5L1). Vertebrate rhodopsin forms a metastable active state (meta II) that inefficiently reverts to the dark state, while bistable opsins can photoconvert between dark and active states.
evaluation: Claims C1-C32 establish well-documented background knowledge about opsin classification and photoreaction properties, supported by multiple citations to established literature. These claims provide the scientific context for the study and are consistently supported by prior work in the field.

result: The authors previously identified Opn5L1 as a novel photocycle opsin. Opn5L1 binds all-trans retinal in the dark to form an active state, and light irradiation suppresses G protein activation through photoisomerization to 11-cis retinal, followed by covalent adduct formation with Cys188. The cysteine at position 188 is well conserved in Opn5L1 but rare in other opsins, supporting its importance for photocyclic function.
evaluation: Claims C33-C41 describe the authors' prior work on Opn5L1, supported by citation to Sato et al., 2018. The sequence conservation analysis (C40-C41) provides additional support for the functional importance of Cys188, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

result: Vertebrate rhodopsin and cone pigments have glycine at position 188, and the molecular mechanism underlying opsin diversification remains unknown.
evaluation: Claims C42 and C7 establish the knowledge gap that motivates the study. C42 is supported by sequence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and C7 accurately describes the state of the field.

result: G188C mutant has much lower thermal stability than wild-type, gradually decaying at 37°C, while wild-type remains stable. Introduction of N2C/D282C mutations improved the thermal stability of G188C mutant.
evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are directly supported by spectroscopic data in Figures 1A-C. The thermal instability of G188C and stabilization by N2C/D282C are clearly demonstrated through time-dependent spectral measurements at 37°C.

result: G188C/N2C/D282C mutant exhibits thermal recovery to the original dark state after photoactivation. Upon yellow light irradiation, the spectrum shifts to UV (meta II formation), then during dark incubation, absorbance decreases in UV and increases at 485 nm. HPLC analysis confirms retinal isomerization from all-trans back to 11-cis during dark incubation.
evaluation: Claims C52-C64 describe the photocyclic property of G188C mutant, supported by spectroscopic data (Figures 1E-G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and HPLC retinal configuration analysis (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 4). The data clearly demonstrate thermal recovery of the dark state, a key finding distinguishing this mutant from wild-type.

result: Wild-type rhodopsin forms meta II upon yellow light irradiation at 0°C, and subsequent UV light produces meta III (λmax ~470 nm) rather than the dark state. Fitting analysis and HPLC data confirm that UV light induces syn/anti isomerization of the Schiff base more efficiently than cis/trans isomerization of retinal.
evaluation: Claims C65-C70 characterize wild-type photoreaction as a control, supported by spectroscopic data (Figure 2A), fitting analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Table 1), and HPLC analysis (Figure 2C). The data confirm established knowledge about wild-type rhodopsin photochemistry.

result: G188C mutant exhibits photoreversibility at 0°C. UV light irradiation of meta II shifts the spectrum back to the visible region with λmax similar to the dark state, and yellow light reirradiation regenerates meta II. Fitting analysis shows the dark state forms more efficiently than meta III, and HPLC confirms efficient 11-cis retinal formation.
evaluation: Claims C71-C77 demonstrate photoreversibility of G188C mutant, supported by spectroscopic data (Figure 2B), fitting analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Table 1), and HPLC data (Figure 2D). The mirror-image spectral changes and efficient dark state recovery distinguish G188C from wild-type.

result: G188C mutant shows light-dependent Gi activation equivalent to wild-type. UV light irradiation suppresses Gi activation, and yellow light reirradiation restores it, consistent with spectral and retinal configuration changes.
evaluation: Claims C78-C82 demonstrate functional consequences of photoreversibility, supported by GTPγS-binding assays (Figure 2E-F). The light-dependent modulation of G protein activation correlates with spectral changes, confirming functional photoreversibility.

result: G188C/N2C/D282C mutant exhibits interconvertibility between dark state and meta II upon alternating yellow and UV light irradiation at 0°C.
evaluation: Claims C83-C84 are supported by spectroscopic data in Figure 2G, demonstrating repeated photoreversibility in the stabilized mutant.

result: Eight other G188 mutants (A, D, M, N, Q, S, T, V) show spectral shifts upon light irradiation, but recovery to the dark state upon UV light occurs most efficiently in G188C mutant.
evaluation: Claims C85-C86 are supported by spectroscopic data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, C) and fitting analysis (Table 1). The comparison demonstrates that cysteine at position 188 is uniquely effective for photoreversibility.

result: E122Q mutation accelerates meta II decay. E122Q/G188C/N2C/D282C mutant shows thermal recovery at 0°C and photocycles ~12 times faster than G188C/N2C/D282C at 37°C (time constants: 5.1 s vs 57.4 s).
evaluation: Claims C87-C90, C153 demonstrate tunable photocycle kinetics, supported by spectroscopic data (Figure 3A-D) and HPLC analysis (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The acceleration of the photocycle by E122Q mutation is well-documented and successfully applied here.

result: In cultured cells, G188C/N2C/D282C mutant shows rapid cAMP recovery after light-induced decrease, faster than N2C/D282C control. E122Q/G188C/N2C/D282C shows even faster recovery. The photocyclic property changes G protein activation profiles by promoting fast recovery to the dark state.
evaluation: Claims C91-C96 demonstrate functional consequences in cells, supported by GloSensor cAMP assays (Figure 4A-G). The differential recovery kinetics between mutants correlate with their photocycle rates, confirming that photocyclic properties modulate cellular signaling.

result: G188C mutant forms photopigments after reconstitution with all-trans retinal, incorporating predominantly 11-cis and 9-cis retinals. The photoreaction is similar to G188C reconstituted with 11-cis retinal. Wild-type shows minimal pigment formation with all-trans retinal.
evaluation: Claims C97-C102 demonstrate unique all-trans retinal binding by G188C, supported by spectroscopic data (Figure 5A-B) and HPLC analysis (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). This suggests thermal isomerization of all-trans to cis retinals within the protein.

result: G188C/N2C/D282C regenerates efficiently with both 11-cis and all-trans retinal, while N2C/D282C shows minimal regeneration with all-trans retinal. G188C mutant uniquely forms photopigments with both retinal isomers.
evaluation: Claims C103-C108 are supported by regeneration experiments (Figure 5D-L). The differential regeneration with all-trans retinal between G188C/N2C/D282C and N2C/D282C demonstrates the unique property of the G188C mutation.

result: Wild-type rhodopsin preferentially converts meta II to meta III rather than the dark state. G188C mutant reverts to the dark state much more efficiently, possibly due to preferential all-trans to 11-cis isomerization in the chromophore-binding pocket.
evaluation: Claims C109-C114 provide mechanistic interpretation supported by experimental data comparing wild-type and G188C photoreactions. C114 is appropriately labeled as speculative, acknowledging uncertainty in the detailed mechanism.

result: Molecular modeling suggests Cys188 is located near the C11=C12 position of retinal and Glu181. During meta II formation, Cys188, Glu181, and water approach the Schiff base, while Glu113 and Ser186 move away. Glu113 and Glu181 serve as counterions in the dark state and meta I, respectively.
evaluation: Claims C115-C117, C120-C121 provide structural context based on crystal structures (Choe et al., 2011; Okada et al., 2004) shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B. The modeling is appropriately based on established structures and cited literature.

result: G188D mutant forms substantial meta I after light irradiation, possibly due to stabilization of the protonated Schiff base by the aspartic acid residue.
evaluation: Claims C118-C119 are supported by spectroscopic data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). C119 appropriately presents the explanation as speculative.

result: The cysteine at position 188 may disturb the local structure and hydrogen-bonding network around the Schiff base and Glu181 in meta II, preventing syn/anti isomerization of the Schiff base C=N double bond.
evaluation: Claims C122-C123 present a mechanistic hypothesis. While C122 cites established knowledge, C123 is speculative and lacks direct experimental validation. The hypothesis is reasonable but requires additional structural or computational studies for confirmation.

result: 9-cis or 11-cis retinal formation from all-trans retinal likely occurs inside G188C mutant, consistent with accelerated thermal cis/trans isomerization in meta II.
evaluation: Claims C124-C125 provide a reasonable inference from the all-trans retinal reconstitution data (Figure 5). The conclusion that isomerization occurs inside the protein is supported by the observation that wild-type does not show this property.

result: T188C mutation of bistable opsin Opn5m induces photocyclic properties. Thermal recovery was observed only in G188C mutant, not other G188 mutants, suggesting cysteine at position 188 has a special role in facilitating thermal retinal isomerization.
evaluation: Claims C126-C128 are supported by citation to recent work (Fujiyabu et al., 2022) and comparison data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The specificity of cysteine for thermal recovery is well-demonstrated.

result: In Opn5L1, Cys188-retinal adduct formation is detected by absorbance increase at 270 nm. This is not observed in G188C rhodopsin mutant. The detailed mechanism of thermal recovery in G188C remains unknown, but may involve transient adduct formation.
evaluation: Claims C129-C133 appropriately acknowledge uncertainty in the mechanism. The absence of 270 nm absorbance increase (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C-D) distinguishes G188C from Opn5L1, and C133 appropriately presents the adduct hypothesis as speculative.

result: By analogy with channelrhodopsins, where a cysteine near C13 modulates photocycle rate without adduct formation, Cys188 in G188C may influence retinal structure and charge distribution to trigger thermal cis/trans isomerization.
evaluation: Claims C134-C135 present an alternative mechanistic hypothesis based on analogy with channelrhodopsins (cited literature). While C134 is established knowledge, C135 is speculative and lacks direct experimental support. The hypothesis is plausible but requires validation.

result: Most bistable opsins have threonine or serine at position 188. The authors speculate ancestral bistable opsins had Thr/Ser at 188, mutated to Gly in monostable opsins. However, G188T or G188S mutations alone do not create bistable opsins, indicating additional residues are necessary.
evaluation: Claims C136-C141 combine sequence analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), evolutionary speculation (C137-C138), supporting evidence from Opn5m (C139), and negative results (C140-C141, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Table 1). The conclusion that additional residues are needed is appropriately supported by the failure to create bistable opsins with single mutations.

result: The main finding: G188C mutation confers photocyclic and photoreversible properties to vertebrate rhodopsin. The mutant's active state (meta II) can revert to the dark state both thermally and photochemically. Position 188 regulates recovery from the active state to the dark state.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9, C43-C46, C142-C143 state the central findings, comprehensively supported by spectroscopic data (Figures 1-2), HPLC analysis (retinal configurations), G protein activation assays, and cellular cAMP measurements. The convergence of multiple experimental approaches strongly supports these conclusions.

result: Position 188 has received little attention in opsins. Combining position 188 mutations with other mutations could enable interconversion of opsin properties. G188C mutant has advantages as an optogenetic tool: all-trans retinal reconstitution, photocyclic properties, high expression, and high G protein activation. Photocycle rate can be modulated by altering meta II lifetime.
evaluation: Claims C144-C152 discuss implications and applications. The optogenetic potential (C146-C150) is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript. C151 is supported by the E122Q results (Figure 3). C145 and C152 appropriately present future directions as speculative.

result: Additional background: Wild-type rhodopsin dark state, meta II, and meta III contain 11-cis-15-anti, all-trans-15-anti, and all-trans-15-syn retinal, respectively. Opn5L1 has Cys at 188; vertebrate visual pigments have Gly. Glu113 and Glu181 are counterions in dark state and meta I.
evaluation: Claims C154-C157 provide additional background information, supported by citations and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A. These are well-established facts that contextualize the study.
